entities.summary:
The Man'yōshū is the oldest existing collection of Japanese poetry, compiled sometime after 759 AD during the Nara period. Created c. 759, this seminal work showcases the earliest form of Japanese poetry, which was heavily influenced by Chinese and Korean poetry of the time. The collection was compiled by the Imperial Court of Japan, with the assistance of many scholars and poets, including the famous poet and scholar, Ōtomo no Yakamochi.


The Man'yōshū contains 3,096 tanka poems, which were written on various topics, including love, nature, and the changing seasons. The poems are characterized by their use of imagery, symbolism, and metaphor, and are considered to be some of the most beautiful and expressive in Japanese literature. The collection was compiled during a time of great cultural and artistic achievement in Japan, and its influence can still be seen in Japanese literature and art today.


The legacy of the Man'yōshū can be seen in the many poets and writers who were inspired by its beauty and expressiveness. The collection has also been an important influence on Western literature, with many poets and writers drawing on its imagery and themes in their own work. Today, the Man'yōshū is considered a national treasure in Japan, and its poems continue to be studied and admired by scholars and readers around the world.
